question:
Patient note:
A 60-year-old man presented to the outpatient internal medicine clinic this morning for evaluation of progressively worsening exertional shortness of breath and lower-extremity edema noted over the past three weeks. He reports that during childhood he was diagnosed with asthma, which evolved into what his pulmonologist has called chronic obstructive airway disease; he now requires a tiotropium inhaler each morning and an albuterol metered-dose inhaler several times per week, especially during changes in the weather. He describes daily sputum production of thick, whitish mucus and audible wheezing that limits his ability to climb one flight of stairs without pausing. He has never required invasive ventilation, but he was hospitalized for an acute exacerbation two winters ago after contracting influenza. He denies any prior episode of crushing substernal chest pain, prolonged diaphoresis, or emergency cardiac catheterization, and he is unaware of any history of circulation problems in his arms or legs; he states that he can walk six city blocks without calf pain, and he has never noticed skin ulcerations of his feet or coldness in his toes. He has never had a focal neurologic deficit, slurred speech, facial droop, or sudden unilateral weakness, and no clinician has told him that he suffered a stroke. On review of systems he denies hematemesis, melena, epigastric burning, or chronic abdominal discomfort, and he has not experienced jaundice, dark urine, abdominal distention, or confusion suggestive of advanced liver dysfunction. Approximately eight years ago, routine blood work revealed a fasting glucose of 118 mg/dL; at that time his primary care provider recommended diet modification and weight reduction, and he has been able to keep readings in the low one-hundreds without pharmacologic agents. Of greater concern, he was informed three years ago that his kidney function had declined: his last documented serum creatinine six months prior was 3.1 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 mL/min/1.73 m², and he has longstanding microalbuminuria. He denies hematuria, flank pain, urinary frequency, nephrolithiasis, or prior dialysis. He has not been diagnosed with any form of malignant disease, hematologic or otherwise, and he has tested negative for HIV on employment screening. Past surgical history is limited to an uncomplicated inguinal hernia repair at age 45. Current medications include fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 µg one inhalation twice daily, tiotropium 18 µg inhalation daily, albuterol 90 µg two puffs as needed, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily suggested by his previous physician “for heart protection,” and cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily. He specifically is not taking any oral hypoglycemic agents, insulin, anticoagulants, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. He was born in the United States, resides alone, and works part-time as an accountant. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily from age 17 until he quit at 57, totaling nearly 80 pack-years; he drinks two to three cans of beer on weekends and denies recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a father who died at 72 of presumed cardiac arrest and a mother living with osteoporosis. On physical examination today he appears chronically ill yet in no acute distress, with a body mass index of 28 kg/m². Blood pressure is 136/78 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 per minute, temperature 36.8 °C orally, and oxygen saturation 92 % on room air at rest dropping to 88 % after a brief corridor walk. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and no bruits are audible. Cardiac auscultation reveals a regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs exhibit diminished breath sounds bilaterally with scattered expiratory wheezes and prolonged expiratory phase; no crackles are appreciated. Peripheral pulses are 2+ and symmetric, without bruits over femoral arteries. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and without organomegaly; no spider angiomata or caput medusae are present. Neurologic examination shows full strength and intact sensation in all four extremities, normal speech, and no pronator drift. Laboratory data sent this morning demonstrate hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, platelets 210 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 46 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, fasting glucose 109 mg/dL, AST 24 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, and total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL. Chest radiograph performed this visit shows hyperinflated lungs without focal consolidation, normal cardiac silhouette, and clear costophrenic angles. Electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm, no Q waves, and no ST-T changes suggestive of prior transmural injury. Ankle-brachial indices performed last year were reported as normal. The patient is here today to discuss his declining exercise tolerance and to formulate a management plan that addresses both pulmonary symptoms and worsening renal function while considering preventive strategies for cardiovascular health.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adds age points to the weights of qualifying chronic conditions.
- Age: the 60–69 band gives 2 points; he is 60 = 2.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: documented chronic obstructive airway disease requiring maintenance inhalers = 1.
- Moderate-to-severe renal disease: chronic creatinine elevation (3.1 mg/dL previously, 3.3 mg/dL now) exceeds the 3 mg/dL threshold = 2.
- Other conditions: impaired fasting glucose is not diagnosed diabetes, and dyspnea and edema alone do not establish heart failure. No other qualifying condition is documented = 0.
Sum: 2 + 1 + 2 + 0 = 5.
Final answer: 5
